title: Neurotransmitter Systems & Plasticity
summary: The brain's chemical highways and how synapses learn.

lessons.title: Glutamate & GABA: Excitation vs Inhibition

levels.kid:
Your brain has a "go" signal and a "stop" signal.

The "go" signal is called **glutamate**. When one brain cell squirts glutamate at the next one, it says, "Wake up and pass the message on!"

The "stop" signal is called **GABA**. It says, "Shh, calm down, don't pass it on."

Think of a car. Glutamate is the gas pedal and GABA is the brake. You need both! Too much gas and the car zooms out of control. That can cause a seizure, when brain cells all fire at once. Too much brake and the car stops, and you get very sleepy.

A healthy brain keeps the gas and the brake balanced all day long.
levels.hs:
Most fast signaling in the brain uses just two chemicals.

**Glutamate** is the main excitatory neurotransmitter. When it binds receptors on the next neuron, it lets positive ions (mostly Na+, sometimes Ca2+) flow in. That nudges the neuron toward firing an action potential. Roughly 80–90% of synapses in the cortex use glutamate.

**GABA** (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. Its receptors usually let chloride (Cl-) in or potassium (K+) out, which makes the inside of the neuron more negative and harder to fire. In the spinal cord and brainstem, **glycine** does a similar inhibitory job.

Fun fact: neurons make GABA *from* glutamate, using an enzyme called glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD).

Why balance matters:
- Too much excitation: seizures, and in stroke, cells literally excited to death (excitotoxicity).
- Too much inhibition: sedation, slowed breathing, coma.

Many drugs work by tipping this balance. Benzodiazepines and barbiturates make GABA receptors work harder, which is why they calm anxiety and stop seizures.
levels.college:
Glutamate and GABA account for the large majority of fast synaptic transmission in the CNS.

**Glutamate receptors**
- **Ionotropic**: AMPA (Na+/K+, fast EPSPs), kainate, and **NMDA**. NMDA receptors pass Na+ and Ca2+, need glycine or D-serine as a co-agonist, and are blocked by Mg2+ at resting potential. They open only when the membrane is already depolarized AND glutamate is bound, making them **coincidence detectors**.
- **Metabotropic (mGluR1–8)**: G-protein coupled, grouped I–III; they modulate excitability and release more slowly.

**Clearance**: excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs), largely on astrocytes, take glutamate up. Astrocytes convert it to glutamine, which goes back to neurons and is turned into glutamate again (the **glutamate–glutamine cycle**).

**GABA receptors**
- **GABA-A**: a pentameric Cl- channel. Benzodiazepines bind at the alpha–gamma interface and increase channel opening *frequency*; barbiturates increase opening *duration* and at high levels open the channel directly. Ethanol, propofol, etomidate and neurosteroids also potentiate GABA-A.
- **GABA-B**: metabotropic (Gi/o), opens K+ channels postsynaptically and reduces Ca2+ entry presynaptically. Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist used for spasticity.

GABA is synthesized from glutamate by GAD (needs vitamin B6, pyridoxal phosphate) and cleared by GAT transporters; GABA transaminase breaks it down. Vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase; tiagabine blocks GAT-1.

**Glycine** receptors (Cl- channels) dominate inhibition in the spinal cord. Strychnine blocks them; tetanus toxin blocks glycine and GABA release from spinal inhibitory interneurons, causing rigid spasms.

**Excitotoxicity**: excess glutamate overactivates NMDA receptors, Ca2+ floods in, and calcium-dependent enzymes and mitochondrial failure kill the cell, central to ischemic injury.
levels.phd:
The excitation–inhibition (E/I) balance is less a fixed ratio than a dynamic, tightly tracked relationship: in cortex, excitatory and inhibitory conductances co-vary on millisecond timescales, with inhibition lagging excitation by a few milliseconds. This creates a narrow temporal window for spike generation and sharpens timing precision.

**NMDA receptor biophysics** underlies much of the theory. The voltage-dependent Mg2+ block gives NMDA current a region of negative slope conductance, so NMDA receptors can support plateau potentials and dendritic NMDA spikes. Subunit composition matters: GluN2B-containing receptors (dominant early in development) have slower deactivation than GluN2A-containing ones; the developmental 2B→2A switch shortens integration windows. Synaptic versus extrasynaptic NMDA receptor activation has been linked to opposing signaling outcomes (CREB activation and survival versus CREB shutoff and death), a framework for selective excitotoxicity, though the strict dichotomy is debated.

**GABA-A diversity**: about 19 subunits assemble mainly as 2alpha:2beta:1gamma. Alpha1-containing receptors are linked to sedation, alpha2/3 to anxiolysis, alpha5 to hippocampal tonic inhibition and memory. Extrasynaptic delta-containing receptors mediate **tonic inhibition** and are especially sensitive to neurosteroids.

**Chloride homeostasis**: GABA-A inhibition depends on low intracellular Cl-, set by KCC2 (extrusion) versus NKCC1 (uptake). In immature neurons NKCC1 dominates, Cl- is high, and GABA is depolarizing. KCC2 downregulation after injury or in epileptic tissue may make GABA less inhibitory or even excitatory, one proposed reason benzodiazepines lose efficacy in prolonged status epilepticus (alongside activity-dependent internalization of synaptic GABA-A receptors and an increase in surface NMDA receptors).

**Interneuron diversity**: parvalbumin-positive basket cells (perisomatic, fast-spiking, gamma rhythms), somatostatin-positive cells (dendritic inhibition), and VIP cells (disinhibition by inhibiting SST cells) form canonical microcircuits. Loss-of-function in the Nav1.1 channel (SCN1A) preferentially impairs interneurons, explaining why Dravet syndrome causes seizures and why sodium-channel blockers can worsen it.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, E/I balance is the logic behind seizures, anesthesia, withdrawal, and much of neurocritical care.

**Status epilepticus**: benzodiazepines are first line because GABA-A potentiation works best early. As seizures persist, synaptic GABA-A receptors are internalized and NMDA receptors move to the surface, so efficacy falls with time. That is why guidelines push fast first-line treatment, then a second-line agent (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate), then anesthetic infusions for refractory cases.

**Alcohol withdrawal**: chronic ethanol potentiates GABA-A and inhibits NMDA. The brain compensates by down-regulating GABA function and up-regulating NMDA. Remove alcohol and you get unopposed excitation: tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, delirium tremens. Benzodiazepines substitute for the missing GABA effect.

**Pitfalls**
- Sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) can worsen seizures in Dravet syndrome and some generalized epilepsies (myoclonic, absence).
- Vigabatrin causes permanent concentric visual field loss, so it needs visual monitoring.
- Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines but can precipitate seizures in chronic users or mixed overdoses; it is not a routine coma cocktail.
- Abrupt baclofen withdrawal (especially from an intrathecal pump failure) can cause high fever, rigidity, seizures and death; treat it as an emergency.

**Neurosurgical relevance**: in traumatic brain injury and subarachnoid hemorrhage, microdialysis studies show surges of extracellular glutamate that correlate with worse outcome, and cortical spreading depolarizations propagate through injured tissue. Seizures after craniotomy or with cortical lesions are common enough that prophylaxis and EEG monitoring are routine considerations. Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis (often with ovarian teratoma) shows what happens when antibodies strip NMDA receptors from synapses: psychiatric symptoms, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability.

keyPoints: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter; GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain (glycine in spinal cord/brainstem)
NMDA receptors need glutamate + co-agonist + depolarization to relieve Mg2+ block: coincidence detectors
GABA-A is a Cl- channel; benzodiazepines increase opening frequency, barbiturates increase duration
GABA is made from glutamate by GAD (needs vitamin B6)
Excess glutamate causes excitotoxicity via Ca2+ influx, central to stroke injury

test.q: What is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain?
test.explain: Glutamate drives most fast excitatory synapses. GABA and glycine are inhibitory; dopamine is a modulator.

test.q: What blocks the NMDA receptor channel at resting membrane potential?
test.explain: Mg2+ sits in the pore at rest; depolarization expels it so Na+ and Ca2+ can flow.

test.q: Benzodiazepines act on GABA-A receptors by:
choices: Increasing how often the channel opens
Increasing how long the channel stays open
test.explain: Benzodiazepines increase opening frequency (and need GABA present). Barbiturates increase opening duration.

test.q: Which ion mainly flows through GABA-A receptors?
test.explain: GABA-A is a ligand-gated chloride channel; Cl- influx usually hyperpolarizes the neuron.

test.q: GABA is made from glutamate by the enzyme glutamic acid ___ (GAD).
test.explain: Glutamic acid decarboxylase removes a carboxyl group from glutamate to make GABA; it needs pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).

test.q: In the spinal cord, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter alongside GABA is:
test.explain: Glycine dominates inhibition in the spinal cord and brainstem; strychnine blocks its receptor.

test.q: What term describes neurons dying from overactivation by glutamate?
test.explain: Excess glutamate overstimulates NMDA receptors, causing toxic Ca2+ overload and cell death, important in stroke and brain trauma.

test.q: Baclofen, used for spasticity, is an agonist at which receptor?
test.explain: Baclofen activates metabotropic GABA-B receptors, reducing excitability in the spinal cord.

test.q: Why is the NMDA receptor called a 'coincidence detector'?
choices: It measures time between action potentials
It fires every time any synapse is active
It opens only when glutamate is bound AND the membrane is depolarized
It detects two neurotransmitters at once by chance
test.explain: NMDA needs both presynaptic glutamate and postsynaptic depolarization (to remove Mg2+), linking input and output activity.

test.q: Tetanus toxin causes muscle rigidity by blocking release of GABA and ___ from spinal inhibitory interneurons.
test.explain: Without inhibitory glycine and GABA release, motor neurons fire unchecked: lockjaw and spasms.

test.q: Which cells take up most synaptic glutamate and recycle it as glutamine?
test.explain: Astrocytic EAAT transporters clear glutamate; glutamine synthetase converts it to glutamine for return to neurons.

test.q: Name the Alzheimer's drug that blocks NMDA receptor channels.
test.explain: Memantine is a moderate-affinity NMDA channel blocker used in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease.

kidTest.q: Glutamate is like the car's...
kidTest.explain: Glutamate says 'go!' and excites the next brain cell.

kidTest.q: GABA is like the car's...
kidTest.explain: GABA says 'stop' and calms brain cells down.

kidTest.q: What can happen if there is way too much 'go' signal?
kidTest.explain: Too much excitement makes many brain cells fire together, which can cause a seizure.

kidTest.q: Too much 'stop' signal makes you feel...
kidTest.explain: Too much GABA calms the brain so much you get very sleepy.

kidTest.q: What is the brain's main 'stop' signal called?
kidTest.explain: GABA is the main calming (inhibitory) chemical in the brain.

kidTest.q: A healthy brain keeps go and stop...
kidTest.explain: Balance keeps the brain working well.

advancedTest.q: Why can benzodiazepines lose effectiveness as status epilepticus continues?
choices: Synaptic GABA-A receptors are internalized while NMDA receptors increase at the surface
The liver destroys them faster during seizures
advancedTest.explain: Prolonged seizures trigger GABA-A receptor endocytosis and NMDA receptor trafficking to the membrane, shifting pharmacologic targets; hence early treatment and NMDA antagonists later.

advancedTest.q: In immature neurons GABA can be depolarizing mainly because:
choices: NKCC1 dominates over KCC2, so intracellular Cl- is high
GABA-A receptors pass Na+ in neonates
advancedTest.explain: High intracellular chloride (NKCC1 uptake, little KCC2 extrusion) shifts the Cl- reversal potential positive, so opening GABA-A channels lets Cl- out and depolarizes.

advancedTest.q: A child with Dravet syndrome (SCN1A loss of function) has worsening seizures on carbamazepine. Best explanation?
choices: Nav1.1 loss mostly impairs inhibitory interneurons; further Na+ channel block reduces inhibition more
advancedTest.explain: Nav1.1 is critical for fast-spiking interneurons; sodium-channel blockers further suppress already weak inhibition.

advancedTest.q: Which disorder involves antibodies against a glutamate receptor, causing psychiatric symptoms, seizures and dyskinesias, often with an ovarian teratoma?
advancedTest.explain: Antibodies to the GluN1 subunit cause receptor internalization; teratomas containing neural tissue can trigger it.

lessons.title: Dopamine Pathways

levels.kid:
**Dopamine** is a brain messenger that helps you move and helps you want things.

It is made in a few small spots deep in the brain and sent out along long roads, like trucks from a factory.

One road goes to the part that helps you move smoothly. If those dopamine cells get sick, people shake and move slowly. That is called Parkinson's disease.

Another road goes to the part that says "Ooh, I want that!" It helps you feel driven to get a snack, finish a game, or learn something new.

A third little road tells another gland to stop making a milk-making hormone.

So dopamine is like a coach: "Move! Go get it!"
levels.hs:
Dopamine is a monoamine neurotransmitter made from the amino acid tyrosine (tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine). Only a few clusters of neurons make it, but they project widely along four classic pathways:

- **Nigrostriatal**: substantia nigra pars compacta → striatum (caudate and putamen). Controls movement. Losing these neurons causes **Parkinson's disease**: tremor at rest, rigidity, slowness (bradykinesia).
- **Mesolimbic**: ventral tegmental area (VTA) → nucleus accumbens. Reward, motivation and learning from surprises. Overactivity here is linked to the "positive" symptoms of psychosis, like hallucinations.
- **Mesocortical**: VTA → prefrontal cortex. Attention, planning, working memory. Underactivity is linked to "negative" symptoms of schizophrenia (flat emotion, low motivation).
- **Tuberoinfundibular**: hypothalamus → pituitary. Dopamine here *inhibits* the release of prolactin.

Drugs show why the pathways matter. Antipsychotics block D2 receptors: that calms mesolimbic overactivity, but blocking the same receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway can cause Parkinson-like stiffness, and blocking them in the tuberoinfundibular pathway raises prolactin. Treating Parkinson's with L-DOPA does the opposite and can sometimes cause hallucinations.

Dopamine is not simply a "pleasure chemical": it is better thought of as a signal for motivation and for learning what is worth pursuing.
levels.college:
**Synthesis and clearance**: tyrosine hydroxylase (rate-limiting, needs tetrahydrobiopterin) converts tyrosine to L-DOPA; aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) makes dopamine. Vesicles load it via VMAT2. Dopamine is cleared by the dopamine transporter (DAT) and degraded by **MAO-B** and **COMT** to homovanillic acid (HVA).

**Receptors** (all GPCRs)
- **D1-like (D1, D5)**: Gs → increase cAMP.
- **D2-like (D2, D3, D4)**: Gi → decrease cAMP; D2 autoreceptors on terminals reduce release.

**Pathways**
- **Nigrostriatal** (SNc → dorsal striatum): in the basal ganglia, dopamine excites the direct (D1) pathway and inhibits the indirect (D2) pathway. Both effects facilitate movement. Parkinsonism appears when roughly half or more of SNc neurons are lost (estimates vary).
- **Mesolimbic** (VTA → nucleus accumbens, amygdala, hippocampus): reward prediction and incentive salience.
- **Mesocortical** (VTA → prefrontal cortex): executive function; D1 receptors dominate here.
- **Tuberoinfundibular** (arcuate nucleus → median eminence → anterior pituitary): tonic inhibition of prolactin via D2 on lactotrophs.

**Clinical pharmacology**
- **Parkinson's**: L-DOPA (crosses the blood–brain barrier, dopamine does not) plus carbidopa (peripheral AADC inhibitor that does not cross the BBB, reducing peripheral side effects like nausea). Also dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline), COMT inhibitors (entacapone).
- **Antipsychotics**: D2 antagonism. Typical agents cause more extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia) and hyperprolactinemia. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, high CK.
- Dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine and cabergoline treat prolactinomas.
- Antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) block D2 in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, which lies outside the BBB, and can also cause dystonia.
levels.phd:
Dopamine's computational role is best captured by the **reward prediction error** (RPE) hypothesis (Schultz, 1990s): midbrain dopamine neurons burst when outcomes are better than predicted, show no change when outcomes are fully predicted, and pause when expected rewards are omitted. With learning, the burst transfers from the reward to the earliest reliable cue, matching the temporal-difference (TD) error term of reinforcement learning models. Optogenetic studies support a causal teaching role: stimulating dopamine neurons at reward delivery can drive learning, although whether dopamine encodes pure RPE, value, or salience in different subregions remains active debate. Ventral striatal dopamine ramps as animals approach goals, and some dorsal striatal and tail-of-striatum populations respond to novelty or aversive salience, suggesting heterogeneity rather than a single scalar signal.

**Tonic vs phasic**: tonic firing (roughly a few Hz) sets extracellular dopamine levels acting on high-affinity D2 receptors; phasic bursts produce transient high concentrations that preferentially engage lower-affinity D1 receptors. This partly explains how one transmitter supports both "go" and "no-go" learning in basal ganglia models: dopamine bursts strengthen D1 direct-pathway synapses (via D1–PKA facilitating LTP), whereas dips promote D2 indirect-pathway plasticity.

**Parkinson's pathobiology**: SNc neurons are selectively vulnerable, plausibly because of long, extremely branched unmyelinated axons, autonomous pacemaking driven by L-type Cav1.3 channels producing mitochondrial oxidant stress, and cytosolic dopamine oxidation. Alpha-synuclein aggregation (Lewy pathology) and Braak staging propose spread from the olfactory bulb and lower brainstem upward. Ventrolateral tier SNc neurons projecting to the dorsal putamen degenerate first, matching the typical motor onset.

**Receptor nuance**: D2 receptors exist as short (presynaptic autoreceptor-enriched) and long isoforms. Antipsychotic efficacy tracks striatal D2 occupancy, with PET studies suggesting a therapeutic window where extrapyramidal risk rises at higher occupancy. Partial agonists (aripiprazole) and fast-dissociation hypotheses offer alternative routes to lower motor side effects.
levels.expert:
Clinically, every dopamine drug is a trade between pathways, and recognizing pathway side effects is a core skill.

**Parkinson's disease management**
- Early on L-DOPA gives a smooth response (the "honeymoon"). As neurons are lost, buffering capacity falls and patients develop **wearing-off**, on–off fluctuations and peak-dose **dyskinesias**.
- Dopamine agonists cause impulse-control disorders (gambling, shopping, hypersexuality) in a significant minority, plus sleep attacks and edema; screen at every visit.
- Hallucinations in PD: reduce add-on drugs first; if an antipsychotic is needed, quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin, because typical antipsychotics can cause catastrophic worsening of parkinsonism. The same applies to dementia with Lewy bodies, where neuroleptic sensitivity can be severe.
- Abruptly stopping dopaminergic drugs (for example, NPO before surgery) can cause parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, which resembles neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Keep PD medications on schedule perioperatively.

**Neurosurgery: deep brain stimulation (DBS)**
- Targets: subthalamic nucleus (STN) or globus pallidus internus (GPi) for PD; ventral intermediate nucleus of the thalamus (Vim) for essential tremor.
- Best predictor of benefit: a robust response to L-DOPA (except tremor, which can respond to DBS even when L-DOPA response is poor). Symptoms that do not respond to L-DOPA, like gait freezing in the "on" state, usually do not respond to DBS.
- STN DBS often allows medication reduction. Cognitive impairment and untreated psychiatric illness are relative contraindications.

**Pituitary**: a hyperprolactinemic patient on risperidone or metoclopramide may simply have drug effect. Large non-functioning pituitary tumors raise prolactin modestly by compressing the stalk and cutting off dopamine (stalk effect), while true prolactinomas usually cause much higher levels and respond to cabergoline, often avoiding surgery even when large.

**Emergency**: acute dystonia after an antiemetic or antipsychotic (oculogyric crisis, torticollis) responds quickly to anticholinergics (benztropine) or diphenhydramine.

keyPoints: Dopamine synthesis: tyrosine → L-DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting) → dopamine (AADC)
Nigrostriatal: SNc → striatum, movement; its loss causes Parkinson's
Mesolimbic: VTA → nucleus accumbens, reward/motivation; mesocortical: VTA → prefrontal cortex
Tuberoinfundibular dopamine inhibits prolactin release
D1-like receptors are Gs; D2-like are Gi; antipsychotics block D2

test.q: Which pathway degenerates in Parkinson's disease?
test.explain: Substantia nigra pars compacta neurons projecting to the striatum are lost, causing the motor signs.

test.q: The rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine synthesis is:
test.explain: Tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to L-DOPA and controls the overall rate; MAO-B and COMT break dopamine down.

test.q: Dopamine from the tuberoinfundibular pathway does what to prolactin?
test.explain: Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin, so D2 blockers raise prolactin.

test.q: The mesolimbic pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus ___.
test.explain: VTA → nucleus accumbens is the core reward and motivation circuit.

test.q: Why is carbidopa given with L-DOPA?
choices: It blocks peripheral conversion of L-DOPA to dopamine
It inhibits MAO-B in the brain
It helps dopamine cross the blood–brain barrier
test.explain: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral AADC but does not enter the brain, so more L-DOPA reaches the brain and peripheral side effects like nausea drop.

test.q: D2-like receptors are coupled to which G protein?
test.explain: D2, D3 and D4 couple to Gi and lower cAMP; D1 and D5 couple to Gs.

test.q: Name the brain structure (midbrain) whose 'pars compacta' contains the dopamine neurons lost in Parkinson's.
test.explain: Substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) neurons are pigmented with neuromelanin and degenerate in PD.

test.q: A patient on a D2-blocking antipsychotic develops stiffness and slow movement. This is from blockade in which pathway?
test.explain: Blocking striatal D2 receptors mimics dopamine loss and causes drug-induced parkinsonism.

test.q: Which pathway is mainly linked to the positive symptoms of psychosis like hallucinations?
test.explain: Mesolimbic dopamine overactivity is linked to positive symptoms; antipsychotic D2 blockade targets it.

test.q: Dopamine is broken down by MAO-B and ___, producing homovanillic acid.
test.explain: COMT and MAO break down dopamine; COMT inhibitors like entacapone prolong L-DOPA effect.

test.q: Fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and high CK after starting an antipsychotic suggests which syndrome?
test.explain: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a dangerous reaction to D2 blockade; stop the drug and give supportive care.

test.q: Why can't dopamine itself be given to treat Parkinson's?
choices: It is destroyed by stomach acid only
It does not cross the blood–brain barrier
It only acts on D1 receptors
test.explain: Dopamine cannot cross the BBB; its precursor L-DOPA is carried across by amino acid transporters.

kidTest.q: Dopamine helps you...
kidTest.explain: Dopamine helps with smooth movement and motivation.

kidTest.q: When the movement dopamine cells get sick, people may...
kidTest.explain: That is Parkinson's disease.

kidTest.q: What is the disease called when movement dopamine cells are lost? (one word)
kidTest.explain: Parkinson's disease happens when dopamine cells for movement die.

kidTest.q: Dopamine is sent along long paths, like...
choices: Trucks on roads from a factory
kidTest.explain: Dopamine cells sit in small spots and send messages far away along pathways.

kidTest.q: Dopamine makes you feel like saying...
kidTest.explain: Dopamine drives motivation to go get things.

kidTest.q: Dopamine is a...
kidTest.explain: It's a chemical messenger in the brain.

advancedTest.q: A monkey learns a light predicts juice. After learning, juice is unexpectedly withheld. Dopamine neurons at the expected juice time:
choices: Fire at the light only and then burst
advancedTest.explain: Omission of a predicted reward produces a negative prediction error, a dip in firing; after learning the burst occurs at the cue.

advancedTest.q: Best predictor that a Parkinson's patient's bradykinesia and rigidity will improve with STN DBS:
choices: Freezing of gait that persists when 'on'
advancedTest.explain: Levodopa responsiveness predicts DBS benefit for appendicular symptoms; tremor is an exception that can respond even when L-DOPA response is weaker.

advancedTest.q: A patient with Parkinson's and new hallucinations needs an antipsychotic. Which is most appropriate?
advancedTest.explain: Quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin have little striatal D2 blockade; haloperidol and fluphenazine can severely worsen parkinsonism, and metoclopramide is a D2-blocking antiemetic.

advancedTest.q: A large non-functioning pituitary tumor raises prolactin modestly by compressing the stalk. What is this called?
advancedTest.explain: Stalk compression interrupts hypothalamic dopamine delivery, disinhibiting lactotrophs.

lessons.title: Serotonin, Norepinephrine & Acetylcholine Systems

levels.kid:
Besides dopamine, the brain has three more helper messengers that work like sprinklers. Each one starts in a tiny spot and sprays its message over big parts of the brain.

- **Serotonin** comes from a line of cells in the brainstem. It helps with mood, sleep and tummy feelings.
- **Norepinephrine** comes from a small blue spot. It is the "Wake up! Pay attention!" messenger. It goes up when you are surprised or scared.
- **Acetylcholine** helps you focus and remember. It is also the messenger that tells your muscles to move.

When these messengers are out of balance, people can feel sad, worried, or forgetful. Some medicines help by fixing the balance.
levels.hs:
Three more "modulatory" systems start in small clusters of neurons and project across the whole brain, changing how other circuits behave.

**Serotonin (5-HT)**
- Made from tryptophan in the **raphe nuclei** of the brainstem.
- Involved in mood, anxiety, sleep, appetite, pain and nausea. About 90% of the body's serotonin is actually in the gut.
- SSRIs (like fluoxetine and sertraline) block serotonin reuptake and are used for depression and anxiety.

**Norepinephrine (NE)**
- Made from dopamine. The main brain source is the **locus coeruleus** ("blue spot") in the pons.
- Controls alertness, attention, and the fight-or-flight response. Its activity is lowest in REM sleep.

**Acetylcholine (ACh)**
- Made from choline and acetyl-CoA.
- In the brain, the **basal nucleus of Meynert** (basal forebrain) sends ACh to the cortex for attention and memory. In Alzheimer's disease these neurons are lost, so drugs that block ACh breakdown (donepezil) are used.
- Outside the brain, ACh activates muscles at the neuromuscular junction and runs the parasympathetic "rest and digest" system.

Each system has many receptor types, so one chemical can have different effects in different places. That is why one drug can help one symptom and cause a side effect somewhere else.
levels.college:
**Serotonin (5-HT)**
- Synthesis: tryptophan → 5-hydroxytryptophan (tryptophan hydroxylase, rate-limiting) → 5-HT (AADC). Cleared by SERT; degraded by MAO-A to 5-HIAA.
- Source: raphe nuclei. Rostral groups (dorsal and median raphe) project to the forebrain; caudal groups project to the cerebellum and spinal cord (pain modulation, motor tone).
- Receptors: seven families. All are GPCRs except **5-HT3**, a ligand-gated cation channel (blocked by ondansetron for nausea). 5-HT1A: Gi, autoreceptor, anxiolysis (buspirone). 5-HT1B/1D: Gi, cranial vessel constriction and reduced neuropeptide release (triptans). 5-HT2A: Gq, cortical excitation (target of atypical antipsychotics).

**Norepinephrine**
- Synthesis: dopamine → NE by dopamine beta-hydroxylase *inside vesicles*. Cleared by NET; degraded by MAO and COMT to VMA and MHPG.
- Source: **locus coeruleus** (dorsal pons), which projects to virtually all of the CNS; also lateral tegmental groups.
- Receptors: alpha1 (Gq), alpha2 (Gi, presynaptic autoreceptor; clonidine and dexmedetomidine), beta (Gs).
- LC firing tracks arousal: high in wakefulness and stress, low in non-REM sleep, nearly silent in REM.

**Acetylcholine**
- Synthesis: choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). Breakdown in the cleft by acetylcholinesterase; choline is recycled by a high-affinity transporter (rate-limiting step).
- Brain sources: basal forebrain (**nucleus basalis of Meynert** → cortex; medial septum → hippocampus) and pontomesencephalic nuclei (pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental) → thalamus, important for REM sleep and arousal. Striatal cholinergic interneurons balance dopamine.
- Receptors: **nicotinic** (ion channels: neuromuscular junction, autonomic ganglia, CNS) and **muscarinic** M1–M5 (GPCRs).

**Clinical anchors**: Alzheimer's (cholinesterase inhibitors); myasthenia gravis (antibodies to nicotinic receptors at the NMJ); serotonin syndrome (excess 5-HT); depression (SSRIs, SNRIs); ADHD (stimulants and atomoxetine increase NE and dopamine).
levels.phd:
Neuromodulatory systems are increasingly framed computationally rather than as "mood chemicals."

**Locus coeruleus and adaptive gain**: Aston-Jones and Cohen's adaptive gain theory proposes two LC modes. **Phasic** mode (moderate tonic firing with task-locked bursts) supports focused exploitation of a current task; **tonic** mode (high baseline firing, weak phasic responses) promotes disengagement and exploration. Pupil diameter tracks LC activity reasonably well and is used as a non-invasive proxy. NE increases the gain of target neurons' input–output functions, sharpening signal relative to noise. Yu and Dayan proposed that ACh signals expected uncertainty and NE signals unexpected uncertainty, a useful though simplified mapping.

**Acetylcholine and cortical state**: basal forebrain ACh shifts cortex toward desynchronized, high-attention states, enhances thalamocortical (feedforward) input relative to intracortical (feedback) input via presynaptic nicotinic and muscarinic effects, and gates plasticity, for example by pairing nucleus basalis stimulation with tones to reorganize auditory cortex maps. Hippocampal theta rhythm depends partly on medial septal cholinergic and GABAergic projections; ACh is high during active waking and REM, low in slow-wave sleep, which has been proposed to favor encoding versus consolidation respectively (Hasselmo).

**Serotonin's elusive function**: models range from behavioral inhibition and patience (optogenetic activation of dorsal raphe neurons increases waiting for delayed rewards) to aversive prediction or opponency to dopamine. The 5-HT system's receptor diversity (14 or so receptor subtypes) makes a single computational account unlikely. SSRI therapeutic latency of weeks despite immediate reuptake blockade implicates downstream adaptation: 5-HT1A autoreceptor desensitization, neuroplasticity and BDNF signaling, and changes in emotional processing biases. The monoamine-deficiency theory of depression is now considered an oversimplification.

**Volume transmission**: many monoaminergic varicosities lack classical postsynaptic densities, releasing transmitter that diffuses to extrasynaptic receptors. Transmission therefore acts more like a broadcast than a point-to-point wire, matching modulation of network state rather than precise information transfer.
levels.expert:
**Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome** is a classic differential.
- Serotonin syndrome: rapid onset (hours) after adding or increasing a serotonergic drug (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, linezolid, tramadol, triptans with other agents, methylene blue). Hallmarks: **clonus** (inducible, ocular), hyperreflexia worse in the legs, agitation, diarrhea, mydriasis, diaphoresis, hyperthermia. Hunter criteria emphasize clonus. Treatment: stop agents, benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) in moderate cases.
- NMS: slower onset (days), "lead-pipe" rigidity, bradyreflexia, high CK; follows dopamine blockade or dopaminergic withdrawal.

**Cholinergic and anticholinergic toxidromes**
- Cholinergic excess (organophosphates, nerve agents): muscarinic (SLUDGE/DUMBELS: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, bronchorrhea, bradycardia) plus nicotinic (fasciculations, weakness). Treat with atropine for muscarinic effects and pralidoxime to reactivate the enzyme before "aging."
- Anticholinergic: hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, urinary retention, delirium. Important in older patients on multiple anticholinergic drugs; physostigmine reverses it centrally in selected cases.

**Myasthenia gravis**: fatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and limb weakness from antibodies against the nicotinic ACh receptor (or MuSK). Watch for myasthenic crisis with respiratory failure; follow forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, not oxygen saturation, which drops late. Many drugs worsen MG (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, beta-blockers).

**Neurosurgical and ICU relevance**
- Dexmedetomidine (alpha2 agonist acting on the locus coeruleus) provides sedation from which patients can be roused for neuro exams, making it popular in neuro ICU and awake craniotomy.
- Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity after severe TBI: episodic tachycardia, hypertension, fever, sweating and posturing. Treated with beta-blockers (propranolol), alpha2 agonists, opioids and gabapentin.
- Cholinesterase inhibitors used in Alzheimer's can cause bradycardia and syncope; consider them in a fall workup.

keyPoints: Serotonin: from tryptophan in the raphe nuclei; 5-HT3 is the only ionotropic 5-HT receptor
Norepinephrine: from dopamine via dopamine beta-hydroxylase; main source is the locus coeruleus in the pons
Acetylcholine: basal nucleus of Meynert → cortex; lost in Alzheimer's
ACh receptors are nicotinic (ion channels) or muscarinic (GPCRs)
Serotonin syndrome features clonus and hyperreflexia; NMS features rigidity and slow onset

test.q: Where are most serotonin-producing neurons in the brain?
test.explain: Raphe nuclei along the brainstem midline make serotonin. Locus coeruleus makes NE.

test.q: The locus coeruleus, the main source of brain norepinephrine, is located in the:
test.explain: The locus coeruleus sits in the dorsal pons, near the fourth ventricle.

test.q: Serotonin is synthesized from the amino acid ___.
test.explain: Tryptophan hydroxylase converts tryptophan to 5-HTP, then AADC makes serotonin.

test.q: Which serotonin receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel?
test.explain: 5-HT3 is ionotropic; ondansetron blocks it to prevent nausea. The rest are GPCRs.

test.q: Cholinergic neurons projecting to the cortex that are lost in Alzheimer's disease are in the:
test.explain: The basal nucleus of Meynert in the basal forebrain supplies ACh to the cortex.

test.q: Which enzyme converts dopamine to norepinephrine?
test.explain: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase, located inside vesicles, makes NE. PNMT makes epinephrine from NE.

test.q: Name the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft.
test.explain: Acetylcholinesterase hydrolyzes ACh into choline and acetate; inhibitors like donepezil increase ACh.

test.q: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are:
test.explain: Nicotinic receptors are cation channels (NMJ, ganglia, CNS); muscarinic receptors are GPCRs.

test.q: A key physical finding that points to serotonin syndrome rather than NMS is:
choices: Very slow onset over a week
test.explain: Serotonin syndrome causes neuromuscular hyperexcitability (clonus, hyperreflexia); NMS causes rigidity and hyporeflexia.

test.q: Myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against the ___ acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction.
test.explain: Antibodies block and destroy nicotinic receptors, causing fatigable weakness.

test.q: SSRIs work mainly by:
test.explain: SSRIs inhibit SERT, keeping serotonin in the synapse longer.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter system's activity is lowest (nearly silent) during REM sleep: serotonin, norepinephrine, or acetylcholine?
test.explain: Locus coeruleus (and raphe) neurons go nearly silent in REM, while cholinergic activity is high.

kidTest.q: Which messenger helps with mood and sleep?
kidTest.explain: Serotonin helps mood, sleep and tummy feelings.

kidTest.q: Norepinephrine is the messenger that says...
kidTest.explain: It goes up when you are surprised or scared.

kidTest.q: Acetylcholine helps you remember and also tells your ___ to move.
kidTest.explain: Acetylcholine is the messenger from nerves to muscles.

kidTest.q: These messengers spread over the brain like...
kidTest.explain: They start in a small spot and spray their message widely.

kidTest.q: Which messenger helps you focus, remember, and move your muscles?
kidTest.explain: Acetylcholine works in the brain and at muscles.

kidTest.q: Norepinephrine comes from a small spot that is what color?
kidTest.explain: The locus coeruleus means 'blue spot'.

advancedTest.q: Why do SSRIs take weeks to improve mood when they block reuptake within hours?
choices: They must convert to tryptophan first
Downstream adaptations like 5-HT1A autoreceptor desensitization and neuroplastic changes take time
SERT takes weeks to be blocked
advancedTest.explain: Initial autoreceptor activation limits serotonin release; desensitization and plasticity (e.g. BDNF signaling) emerge over weeks.

advancedTest.q: A patient with an organophosphate poisoning has bronchorrhea and fasciculations. Which treatment pair addresses muscarinic effects and enzyme reactivation?
advancedTest.explain: Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects (secretions, bradycardia) but not nicotinic weakness; pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase if given before the enzyme 'ages'.

advancedTest.q: Why is dexmedetomidine attractive for sedation in neuro ICU and awake craniotomy?
choices: It is a strong GABA-A agonist
It allows patients to be roused for neurological exams with little respiratory depression
advancedTest.explain: Alpha2 agonism at the locus coeruleus produces arousable sedation with minimal respiratory depression.

advancedTest.q: In myasthenic crisis, which bedside breathing measurement (abbreviated FVC) is followed rather than oxygen saturation?
advancedTest.explain: Saturation drops late; serial FVC and negative inspiratory force detect neuromuscular respiratory failure early.

lessons.title: Synaptic Plasticity: LTP & LTD

levels.kid:
How do you remember things? Your brain cells change their connections!

Imagine a path through tall grass. The more you walk it, the clearer and easier it gets. Brain connections work the same way. When two brain cells "talk" a lot, the link between them gets stronger. Scientists call that **LTP**, which means the link stays strong for a long time.

When two cells hardly talk, their link gets weaker, like a path the grass grows back over. That is called **LTD**.

Strengthening some paths and weakening others is how you learn to ride a bike, remember a friend's name, or get better at a game. Practice really does change your brain!
levels.hs:
Learning changes the strength of synapses, a property called **synaptic plasticity**. In 1949, Donald Hebb suggested that when one neuron repeatedly helps fire another, the connection between them strengthens, often summarized as "cells that fire together wire together."

**Long-term potentiation (LTP)** was discovered in the hippocampus in 1973 (Bliss and Lømo). A short, strong burst of stimulation made the synapse respond more strongly for hours to weeks.

How it works at a typical hippocampal synapse:
1. Glutamate is released and activates AMPA receptors, which depolarize the cell.
2. If the depolarization is strong enough, Mg2+ pops out of the NMDA receptor channel.
3. Ca2+ rushes in through NMDA receptors.
4. A large Ca2+ signal activates enzymes that add more AMPA receptors to the synapse, so the next signal is bigger.

**Long-term depression (LTD)** is the opposite: low-frequency stimulation causes a small, slow rise in Ca2+, which activates enzymes (phosphatases) that remove AMPA receptors. The synapse weakens.

Both matter. LTP helps store memories; LTD helps erase noise, refine skills and keep the system from saturating. The cerebellum uses LTD to fine-tune movements.

Memory problems in diseases like Alzheimer's are thought to involve damaged synaptic plasticity.
levels.college:
**Properties of NMDA-dependent LTP (CA3 → CA1 Schaffer collaterals)**
- **Cooperativity**: enough inputs must be co-active to depolarize the cell.
- **Associativity**: a weak input paired with a strong one gets potentiated too.
- **Input specificity**: only active synapses are potentiated.

**Mechanism**
- Induction: NMDA receptor Ca2+ influx activates **CaMKII**, which autophosphorylates (Thr286) and stays active after Ca2+ falls. PKC and other kinases contribute.
- Early expression: phosphorylation of AMPA receptor GluA1 increases channel conductance, and more AMPA receptors are inserted into the postsynaptic membrane. "Silent synapses" with NMDA but no AMPA receptors can become functional.
- Late LTP (L-LTP, hours+): requires gene transcription (PKA → CREB) and protein synthesis, and structural growth of dendritic spines.

**LTD**: low-frequency stimulation (e.g. 1 Hz for 15 minutes) produces modest Ca2+ elevation that preferentially activates phosphatases (calcineurin, PP1), dephosphorylating AMPA receptors and driving their endocytosis. The idea that high Ca2+ gives LTP and moderate Ca2+ gives LTD is the **calcium control hypothesis**.

**Other forms**
- **mGluR-dependent LTD** (hippocampus, cerebellum), requiring local protein synthesis.
- **Cerebellar LTD**: concurrent parallel-fiber and climbing-fiber activity depresses parallel fiber → Purkinje synapses; supports motor learning.
- **Presynaptic LTP** at mossy fiber → CA3 synapses is NMDA-independent and cAMP/PKA dependent.
- **Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP)**: presynaptic spike shortly *before* postsynaptic spike → LTP; after → LTD.
- **Homeostatic synaptic scaling**: neurons globally scale synaptic strength up or down to keep firing rates stable.

**Evidence for memory**: blocking NMDA receptors in the hippocampus (e.g. with AP5) impairs spatial learning in the Morris water maze. Patient H.M., after bilateral medial temporal lobe removal, lost the ability to form new declarative memories while learning motor skills normally.
levels.phd:
LTP is a family of phenomena, and the link between it and memory is supported by convergent rather than conclusive evidence.

**Sufficiency and necessity**: occlusion experiments (learning saturates subsequent LTP), mimicry (optogenetically induced LTP at engram synapses creating associations, and optogenetic LTD erasing a fear memory that LTP then restores, Nabavi et al. 2014), and blockade (NMDA antagonists or GluN1 knockout in CA1) together constitute the strongest case. Engram studies (Tonegawa and colleagues) show that reactivating sparse, activity-tagged ensembles can trigger recall, even in amnesia models where spine density is reduced, suggesting memory information may partly reside in connectivity patterns rather than synaptic weights alone.

**Synaptic tagging and capture** (Frey and Morris): weak stimulation sets a local "tag" that can capture plasticity-related proteins produced by strong stimulation elsewhere on the neuron, explaining how input specificity coexists with cell-wide transcription. PKMzeta was proposed as a persistent maintenance kinase (ZIP erasing established memory), but knockout mice maintain LTP and memory, with compensation by PKC iota/lambda; the specificity of ZIP is also questioned. This controversy illustrates the gap between a molecular mechanism and a memory trace.

**Metaplasticity**: the BCM (Bienenstock–Cooper–Munro) rule posits a sliding threshold between LTD and LTP that shifts with prior activity, stabilizing learning. Experimentally, prior activity and the GluN2A/GluN2B ratio shift the threshold, as in visual cortex after dark rearing.

**Systems consolidation**: hippocampal sharp-wave ripples during non-REM sleep replay waking sequences, coordinated with cortical slow oscillations and thalamocortical spindles, proposed to transfer memories to the neocortex. Disrupting ripples impairs consolidation. Standard consolidation theory and multiple trace/trace transformation theory differ on whether the hippocampus is ever fully dispensable for detailed episodic retrieval.

**Pathological plasticity**: maladaptive LTP-like changes in dorsal horn neurons underlie central sensitization in chronic pain; aberrant plasticity contributes to epileptogenesis ("kindling") and to addiction, where drugs of abuse alter AMPA/NMDA ratios in VTA and accumbens neurons.
levels.expert:
Plasticity is the biological basis of nearly all neurological recovery, so clinicians use it, protect it, and sometimes fight it.

**Stroke and brain injury recovery**
- Most spontaneous motor recovery occurs in the first weeks to months, a "sensitive period" with heightened plasticity (growth-promoting genes, reduced inhibition in perilesional cortex). Early, intensive, task-specific rehabilitation exploits this.
- Constraint-induced movement therapy forces use of the affected arm, driving cortical map expansion.
- Diaschisis (depressed function in connected but undamaged regions) resolves partly through plasticity.

**Neurosurgery**
- **Cortical plasticity** allows staged resection of slow-growing low-grade gliomas near eloquent cortex: function can shift to adjacent or homologous areas over time, demonstrated with repeat intraoperative mapping. Awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation maps language and motor function before resection.
- Peripheral nerve transfers (for example, intercostal-to-musculocutaneous for brachial plexus injury) rely on the brain relearning to control a muscle with a donor nerve.
- After hemispherectomy for intractable childhood epilepsy, young children can recover substantial function because of developmental plasticity, more so the younger the child.

**Maladaptive plasticity**
- Chronic pain and central sensitization (allodynia after nerve injury).
- Phantom limb pain correlates with cortical reorganization; mirror therapy has been tried.
- Focal dystonia in musicians may reflect excessive overlapping somatosensory representations.
- Epileptogenesis after injury: a latent period of network rewiring often precedes post-traumatic epilepsy.

**Memory clinic**
- Bilateral hippocampal damage (HSV encephalitis, anoxia, transient global amnesia) produces anterograde amnesia with preserved procedural learning.
- Medications with strong anticholinergic or sedative effects impair encoding, particularly in older patients.
- Repetitive TMS protocols (high-frequency facilitates, low-frequency inhibits) borrow LTP/LTD logic and are approved for treatment-resistant depression.

keyPoints: LTP: lasting strengthening of synapses after strong activity; LTD: lasting weakening after weak activity
Classic LTP at CA3→CA1 needs NMDA receptor Ca2+ influx and CaMKII, then more AMPA receptors
Large Ca2+ rise → kinases → LTP; modest Ca2+ rise → phosphatases → LTD
Late LTP needs gene transcription (CREB) and protein synthesis
Cerebellar LTD at parallel fiber–Purkinje synapses supports motor learning

test.q: LTP was first described in which brain region?
test.explain: Bliss and Lømo described LTP in the rabbit hippocampus in 1973.

test.q: Which receptor's calcium influx is required to induce classic LTP at CA1 synapses?
test.explain: NMDA receptors open only when glutamate binds and Mg2+ is expelled by depolarization, letting Ca2+ in.

test.q: During LTP, more ___ receptors are inserted into the postsynaptic membrane, making responses bigger.
test.explain: AMPA receptor insertion and phosphorylation is the main expression mechanism of early LTP.

test.q: LTD is typically induced by:
test.explain: Prolonged low-frequency stimulation produces modest Ca2+ elevation that activates phosphatases.

test.q: Which kinase becomes persistently active by autophosphorylation and is central to LTP induction?
test.explain: CaMKII autophosphorylates at Thr286 and remains active after Ca2+ falls.

test.q: Late-phase LTP, lasting many hours, specifically requires:
choices: New gene transcription and protein synthesis
test.explain: L-LTP depends on CREB-driven transcription and new protein synthesis.

test.q: Complete Hebb's idea: 'Cells that fire together, ___ together.'
test.explain: Hebb's postulate: correlated firing strengthens the connection.

test.q: Input specificity of LTP means:
choices: Every synapse on the neuron is strengthened
Only the synapses that were active are strengthened
test.explain: Potentiation is restricted to active synapses, allowing each neuron to store many associations.

test.q: In spike-timing-dependent plasticity, a presynaptic spike just BEFORE a postsynaptic spike causes:
test.explain: Pre-before-post timing (tens of ms) produces LTP; post-before-pre produces LTD.

test.q: Cerebellar motor learning involves LTD at parallel fiber synapses onto ___ cells.
test.explain: Co-activation of parallel fibers and climbing fibers depresses parallel fiber → Purkinje synapses.

test.q: Which enzyme type (removes phosphate groups) is preferentially activated during LTD?
test.explain: Modest Ca2+ activates calcineurin and PP1, which dephosphorylate AMPA receptors and promote their removal.

test.q: Patient H.M. after bilateral medial temporal lobe removal could still:
test.explain: He had severe anterograde amnesia for declarative memory, but procedural (motor skill) learning was preserved.

kidTest.q: When two brain cells talk a lot, their link gets...
kidTest.explain: Lots of talking strengthens the connection, like a well-walked path.

kidTest.q: A brain link that is hardly used gets...
kidTest.explain: Unused links fade, like grass growing back over a path.

kidTest.q: Brain links getting stronger is like...
choices: A path getting clearer the more you walk it
kidTest.explain: Practice clears the path.

kidTest.q: What is the short name for links getting stronger for a long time? (3 letters)
kidTest.explain: LTP means long-term potentiation.

kidTest.q: Practicing a game changes your...
kidTest.explain: Practice strengthens the right brain connections.

kidTest.q: LTD means a link gets...
kidTest.explain: LTD is long-term depression: a link weakening.

advancedTest.q: Optogenetically inducing LTD at auditory inputs to the amygdala erased a conditioned fear memory, and inducing LTP restored it. This supports that:
choices: The amygdala is not involved in fear
Synaptic potentiation is necessary and sufficient for that memory
Memory is stored in glia only
advancedTest.explain: Nabavi et al. (2014) showed bidirectional control, strong causal evidence linking LTP to a specific memory.

advancedTest.q: Synaptic tagging and capture explains:
choices: How weakly stimulated synapses can achieve late LTP using proteins made after strong stimulation elsewhere on the same neuron
advancedTest.explain: A local tag set by weak activity captures plasticity proteins produced cell-wide by strong activity.

advancedTest.q: Why can low-grade gliomas near language cortex sometimes be resected in stages with less deficit than expected?
choices: Slow growth allows functional reorganization to adjacent or distant cortex
advancedTest.explain: Slow-growing lesions permit cortical plasticity; repeat awake mapping can show function has shifted, enabling more extensive resection.

advancedTest.q: Name the theory of a sliding threshold between LTD and LTP that shifts with prior activity (abbreviation).
advancedTest.explain: The Bienenstock–Cooper–Munro rule describes metaplasticity: high prior activity raises the LTP threshold.

lessons.title: Neuropeptides & Neuromodulation

levels.kid:
Some brain messengers are tiny and fast, like a quick text message. Others are bigger and slower, like a long letter. The big, slow ones are called **neuropeptides**.

Neuropeptides are made of little chains of building blocks. Brain cells save them up in special bags and only let them out when they are very busy.

Some neuropeptides are amazing:
- **Endorphins** are the body's own painkillers. They help after you get hurt.
- **Oxytocin** helps people feel close and cuddly.
- **Orexin** helps keep you awake.

Instead of saying "go" or "stop" right away, they change the mood of the whole area for a while, like turning the lights down in a room.
levels.hs:
Not all neurotransmitters are small molecules. **Neuropeptides** are short chains of amino acids (from about 3 to over 30) that neurons use as slower, longer-lasting signals.

How they differ from classic transmitters like glutamate:
- **Made differently**: they are built as larger precursor proteins in the cell body, then cut into active pieces and shipped down the axon. Small transmitters are made right at the terminal.
- **Stored differently**: in large dense-core vesicles, released mostly during high-frequency firing.
- **No recycling**: they are broken down by enzymes (peptidases), not taken back up.
- **Slow, broad effects**: they act on G-protein coupled receptors, so effects take longer and last longer.

Important examples:
- **Endorphins, enkephalins and dynorphins** (endogenous opioids): reduce pain. Morphine works by mimicking them.
- **Substance P**: carries pain signals in the spinal cord.
- **Oxytocin and vasopressin**: made in the hypothalamus; social bonding, labor and water balance.
- **Orexin (hypocretin)**: keeps you awake; losing orexin neurons causes **narcolepsy**.
- **Neuropeptide Y**: increases appetite.
- **CGRP**: involved in migraine.

Neuromodulation means changing how a circuit responds rather than directly firing it, like adjusting the volume rather than pressing play.
levels.college:
**Biosynthesis**: neuropeptides are translated as preprohormones in the rough ER, processed in the Golgi, packaged into **large dense-core vesicles (LDCVs)**, and cleaved by prohormone convertases during transport. One precursor can yield several peptides: **POMC** gives ACTH, alpha-MSH and beta-endorphin.

**Release**: LDCVs sit away from active zones and need sustained or high-frequency firing (larger, more widespread Ca2+ rises). Peptides are often **co-released** with a classic transmitter (e.g. glutamate with substance P in nociceptors; GABA with enkephalin in striatal neurons).

**Termination**: diffusion and extracellular peptidases (e.g. neprilysin, ACE); no reuptake. Nanomolar receptor affinity allows action at a distance (volume transmission).

**Key systems**
- **Opioid peptides**: beta-endorphin (mu), enkephalins (delta), dynorphins (kappa). Mu agonism mediates analgesia, respiratory depression, miosis and constipation. The periaqueductal gray–rostral ventromedial medulla pathway provides descending pain inhibition.
- **Substance P / NK1 receptor**: nociception, neurogenic inflammation, vomiting (NK1 antagonist aprepitant is an antiemetic).
- **CGRP**: released from trigeminal afferents, a potent vasodilator; CGRP monoclonal antibodies and gepants treat migraine.
- **Orexin/hypocretin**: lateral hypothalamus, stabilizes wakefulness by exciting monoaminergic and cholinergic arousal centers. Narcolepsy type 1 = loss of orexin neurons, low CSF hypocretin, cataplexy. Orexin antagonists (suvorexant) treat insomnia.
- **Hypothalamic peptides**: CRH (stress axis), TRH, GnRH, somatostatin, oxytocin and vasopressin (magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei release them from the posterior pituitary).
- **Appetite**: NPY/AgRP neurons (hunger) and POMC/CART neurons (satiety) in the arcuate nucleus respond to leptin and ghrelin.

**Neuromodulation** broadly: actions through GPCRs that change excitability, release probability, or plasticity rules rather than directly causing fast synaptic potentials. Monoamines and ACh are also neuromodulators in this sense.
levels.phd:
Neuromodulation solves a fundamental problem: anatomically fixed circuits must produce flexible outputs. The classic demonstration comes from the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (Marder and colleagues). A circuit of about 30 identified neurons generates distinct rhythmic motor patterns depending on which of dozens of modulators bathe it; peptides reconfigure the network by altering intrinsic currents and synaptic strengths. The same work showed that similar network output arises from widely varying combinations of conductances (degeneracy), a principle relevant to why individuals differ in drug responses.

**Peptidergic connectomes**: single-cell transcriptomics in mouse cortex shows that nearly all neurons express at least one neuropeptide precursor and one neuropeptide GPCR, implying dense, overlapping peptide networks layered over the synaptic wiring diagram (Smith et al., 2019). Thus the classical connectome alone underdetermines function.

**Release biophysics**: LDCV fusion depends on CAPS proteins and synaptotagmin isoforms distinct from those at fast synapses; dendritic peptide release (e.g. oxytocin and vasopressin from magnocellular dendrites) can be autonomous of axonal firing and primed by prior signals, enabling long-lasting, self-sustaining hormonal states.

**Opioid receptor signaling** offers a lesson in biased agonism: mu receptor signaling through G proteins was proposed to mediate analgesia while beta-arrestin-2 recruitment mediated respiratory depression and tolerance, motivating "biased" agonists. Later studies questioned this, with respiratory depression persisting in arrestin knockouts, and low intrinsic efficacy rather than bias may explain improved safety profiles.

**Social neuropeptides**: prairie vole pair-bonding depends on oxytocin receptor density in the nucleus accumbens and vasopressin V1a receptors in the ventral pallidum; species differences in receptor distribution (not ligand levels) predict monogamy. Human intranasal oxytocin studies were initially enthusiastic, but replication problems and uncertain CNS penetration temper conclusions.

**Orexin** neurons integrate metabolic signals (glucose, leptin, ghrelin) with arousal, coupling wakefulness to energy needs; their autoimmune loss in narcolepsy (HLA-DQB1*06:02 association, a seasonal link to H1N1 infection and one specific vaccine) illustrates neuroimmunology and peptide circuitry together.
levels.expert:
Neuropeptide pharmacology has moved from theory to some of the most important recent therapies.

**Migraine**
- CGRP pathway drugs: monoclonal antibodies (erenumab against the receptor; fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab against the ligand) for prevention, and gepants (ubrogepant, rimegepant, atogepant) for acute and preventive use.
- Unlike triptans, gepants do not constrict blood vessels, so they are options for patients with cardiovascular disease where triptans are contraindicated.
- Medication overuse headache: frequent use of acute drugs (opioids, combination analgesics, triptans) can worsen headaches.

**Opioids**
- Overdose triad: coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression. Naloxone (competitive mu antagonist) reverses it; its duration can be shorter than the opioid's, so patients need observation for re-sedation.
- In neuro ICU, opioid analgesia and sedation can mask the neuro exam; daily sedation interruption or short-acting agents help.
- Opioid-induced hyperalgesia can paradoxically worsen pain.

**Sleep**
- Narcolepsy type 1: excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter or emotion), sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations. Diagnosis: polysomnography with multiple sleep latency test (mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with 2 or more sleep-onset REM periods) or low CSF hypocretin.
- Hypothalamic lesions (tumors, surgery for craniopharyngioma) can cause secondary narcolepsy and hyperphagic obesity.

**Pituitary and hypothalamus for the neurosurgeon**
- After transsphenoidal surgery or hypothalamic injury, vasopressin disruption causes **diabetes insipidus** (now termed arginine vasopressin deficiency): high-volume dilute urine, rising sodium. It can follow a **triphasic response**: DI, then SIADH-like antidiuresis (release of stored vasopressin from degenerating terminals), then permanent DI.
- SIADH and cerebral salt wasting both cause hyponatremia after SAH; the key difference is volume status (euvolemic or hypervolemic vs hypovolemic), and fluid restriction can be dangerous in salt wasting, risking vasospasm-related ischemia.
- Somatostatin analogues (octreotide) treat acromegaly when surgery does not cure growth hormone excess.

keyPoints: Neuropeptides are short amino-acid chains made from larger precursors in the cell body
Stored in large dense-core vesicles; released with high-frequency firing; no reuptake
Endogenous opioids: beta-endorphin, enkephalins, dynorphins
Orexin (hypocretin) loss causes narcolepsy type 1 with cataplexy
CGRP is a migraine target; vasopressin loss after pituitary surgery causes diabetes insipidus

test.q: Neuropeptides are stored in:
test.explain: Peptides are packaged in large dense-core vesicles; small clear vesicles hold classic transmitters like glutamate.

test.q: How is the action of neuropeptides mainly ended?
test.explain: There is no reuptake; extracellular peptidases and diffusion terminate signaling.

test.q: Loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons causes:
test.explain: Orexin stabilizes wakefulness; loss causes sleepiness and cataplexy.

test.q: The precursor protein POMC is cleaved into ACTH, alpha-MSH and beta-___.
test.explain: Pro-opiomelanocortin yields several peptides, including the opioid beta-endorphin.

test.q: Which peptide's pathway is targeted by new migraine antibodies and gepants?
test.explain: Calcitonin gene-related peptide from trigeminal nerves is central to migraine.

test.q: Neuropeptides usually act on which kind of receptor?
test.explain: Most neuropeptide receptors are GPCRs, producing slower, longer-lasting effects.

test.q: Which peptide carries pain signals in the spinal cord and acts on NK1 receptors?
test.explain: Substance P is co-released with glutamate from nociceptors.

test.q: Neuropeptides are typically released when a neuron:
choices: Fires a single action potential only
Fires at high frequency or in bursts
test.explain: Dense-core vesicles need larger, longer Ca2+ signals from sustained firing.

test.q: Oxytocin and vasopressin are made in the hypothalamus and released from the ___ pituitary.
test.explain: Magnocellular neurons send axons to the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).

test.q: Morphine relieves pain mainly by acting on which receptor?
test.explain: Mu opioid receptors mediate analgesia (and respiratory depression).

test.q: Sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter, seen in narcolepsy type 1, is called what?
test.explain: Cataplexy is REM-sleep atonia intruding into wakefulness.

test.q: What does 'neuromodulation' mean?
choices: Changing how a circuit responds rather than directly firing it
test.explain: Modulators adjust excitability, release and plasticity, like turning the volume rather than pressing play.

kidTest.q: Neuropeptides are messages that are...
kidTest.explain: They are slower, longer-lasting messages.

kidTest.q: Endorphins are the body's own...
kidTest.explain: Endorphins help reduce pain.

kidTest.q: Which neuropeptide helps keep you awake?
kidTest.explain: Orexin keeps you awake.

kidTest.q: Which neuropeptide helps people feel close and cuddly?
kidTest.explain: Oxytocin helps with bonding.

kidTest.q: Neuropeptides change the whole area for a while, like...
choices: Turning the lights down in a room
kidTest.explain: They change the mood of the area slowly.

kidTest.q: Neuropeptides are made of chains of...
kidTest.explain: They are chains of amino acids, tiny building blocks.

advancedTest.q: After transsphenoidal surgery, a patient has polyuria, then low urine output with hyponatremia, then polyuria again. This is:
choices: The triphasic response (DI → SIADH-like phase → permanent DI)
advancedTest.explain: Injury causes DI, then uncontrolled release of stored vasopressin from degenerating terminals, then permanent DI if most magnocellular neurons are lost.

advancedTest.q: A patient with SAH develops hyponatremia with low volume status and high urine sodium. Why is fluid restriction dangerous here?
choices: Fluid restriction raises sodium too fast
SIADH is always treated with fluids
Likely cerebral salt wasting; restricting fluid worsens hypovolemia and vasospasm-related ischemia
advancedTest.explain: Salt wasting is hypovolemic; treatment is volume and sodium replacement, unlike SIADH.

advancedTest.q: Why can a gepant be chosen over a triptan for acute migraine in a patient with coronary disease?
choices: Gepants block CGRP signaling without vasoconstriction
advancedTest.explain: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists that constrict vessels; gepants antagonize the CGRP receptor without vasoconstriction.

advancedTest.q: Which arcuate nucleus neurons co-expressing AgRP drive hunger (abbreviation)?
advancedTest.explain: NPY/AgRP neurons promote feeding; POMC/CART neurons promote satiety; leptin inhibits the former and excites the latter.
